newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Kesri grows from idealist to strongman.
newsitem.headline: India's Kesri grows from idealist to strongman.

text.p: India's veteran Congress party leader Sitaram Kesri is a former follower of Mahatma Gandhi who spent years as a backroom political strategist but is now calling the shots despite his age and formidable opposition within his party.

His swift move to end Congress support to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition on Sunday marked a new high in a political career which has seen him evolve from a Gandhian idealist to a tactician steeped in realpolitik.
As a follower of Gandhi, India's independence leader, Kesri was jailed several times by British colonial rulers.
After a steady rise in the Congress party, Kesri, now 77, was known as "Mr Moneybags" for his ability to raise funds at will while keeping his own bank accounts immaculately clean.

For decades, he hovered close to the top leadership of the party, as a lawmaker, minister and party official. He was Welfare Minister in Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao's government that lost power in last year's general elections.
His election as Congress president last September and as the party's boss in parliament in January threw the self-effacing backroom strategist into the forefront of national politics.
"Age is not with me," the veteran lamented to Reuters earlier this year, his apparent humility belying a tough inner party campaign through which he won control in parliament.

Kesri's unanimous selection by "consensus", without a formal vote, came about in much the same controversial way as the exit of his predecessor, Rao, who resigned reluctantly as Congress president following a court summons in a criminal cheating case.

The party reins glided smoothly into Kesri's soft hands that often stretch out for affectionate handshakes that can be deceptive. Kesri, seen as a staunch Rao loyalist, quietly asserted himself to take control from a defiant Rao.

But Rao's followers struck back after the Congress lost vital seats in a round of parliamentary byelections this year and lost power in the northern state of Punjab to an alliance formed by a regional Sikh party and Hindu nationalists.
Deve Gowda seemed to be secure in the confidence that a weak Congress meant a longer spell in power for his United Front coalition when Kesri threw his bombshell on Sunday.
Kesri has been careful, never wearing his ambition on his sleeves, and gently rallying young party supporters who give him strong backing but pose no challenge to his leadership.
He has also scrupulously avoided a split in the party. He maintained a studied distance from Rao loyalists, but never went too close to Rao's rebellious opponents.
"People who talk about splits do not understand the Congress," Kesri said recently. "It is like a large family in which differences are sorted out collectively."
His philosophical approach has won Kesri the sobriquet of Chacha, or Uncle, among his followers and foes.
Kesri, who speaks faltering English and rustic accented Hindi, was a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi and has a stature that inspires awe even among senior Congressmen.
As a student Kesri, who comes from the mineral-rich but economically backward state of Bihar, quit his studies to join the freedom movement.

Jailed by the British, he refused parole to attend his father's funeral. Many believe Kesri's roots in the movement and his amiable disposition could help him bind togther the party which led India to freedom but now finds its support dwindling.

In a party which rivals say is too strongly oriented towards the Hindu upper castes and the rich, Kesri has been an outspoken supporter of job quotas in government to help lower castes. He also champions protection for minority Moslems.
The challenge before Kesri is to revitalise the party, which ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947.
